clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder of anterior horn (lower motor neuron) degeneration, most commonly caused by homozygous loss of function of the SMN1 gene.
It produces progressive, symmetrical muscle weakness and wasting that is typically more marked proximally and in the legs more than the arms.
Disease severity is graded into types (from severe infantile-onset to milder later-onset forms) and correlates broadly with the number of copies of the modifying SMN2 gene.
Severe infantile SMA (type 1) presents with profound hypotonia, poor head control, a weak cry, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and paradoxical (belly) breathing with a bell-shaped chest.
Tongue fasciculations and absent deep tendon reflexes are characteristic, while cognition and sensation are preserved.
Respiratory muscle and bulbar weakness drive the major morbidity and mortality, particularly recurrent aspiration and respiratory failure in the most severe forms.
Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing showing biallelic SMN1 loss, with SMN2 copy number providing prognostic information.
Disease-modifying therapies that increase SMN protein have substantially changed the outlook, and newborn screening enables early, presymptomatic treatment.
Multidisciplinary supportive care addresses respiratory support, nutrition, orthopaedic complications such as scoliosis and contractures, and physiotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Loss of functional SMN protein, resulting from homozygous deletion or mutation of SMN1, leads to degeneration and loss of the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei. The nearly identical SMN2 gene produces only a small amount of full-length functional protein, so a higher SMN2 copy number partially compensates and mitigates severity. Denervation of skeletal muscle causes progressive weakness and atrophy, with the respiratory and bulbar musculature critically affected in severe forms, resulting in hypoventilation, impaired airway clearance, aspiration, and respiratory failure.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoxic-ischaemic or metabolic encephalopathy causing hypotonia
Prader-Willi syndrome and other central causes of hypotonia
Pompe disease and other metabolic myopathies
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for SMN1 deletion/mutation with SMN2 copy number
Assessment of respiratory function and swallowing safety
Creatine kinase (usually normal or only mildly elevated, helping distinguish from dystrophies)
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies if genetic testing is inconclusive
redFlags: Respiratory failure or hypoventilation from progressive respiratory muscle weakness
Bulbar weakness with unsafe swallowing and recurrent aspiration
Rapidly progressive weakness and loss of motor milestones in an infant
Weak cough and impaired airway clearance during intercurrent respiratory infection
Signs of impending ventilatory decompensation such as paradoxical breathing and rising work of breathing
reference.prognosis: Historically severe infantile-onset disease carried a very poor prognosis with early respiratory failure, while later-onset forms had longer survival with variable disability. Early diagnosis through newborn screening and initiation of SMN-directed disease-modifying therapy have markedly improved motor outcomes and survival, especially when started presymptomatically.
pitfalls: Attributing infantile hypotonia to a central cause and missing the lower motor neuron pattern
Overlooking tongue fasciculations and preserved cognition as clues to anterior horn disease
Underestimating respiratory and bulbar risk, especially during intercurrent illness
Delaying genetic confirmation and thereby missing the window for early therapy
Failing to organise multidisciplinary respiratory, nutritional, and orthopaedic support
management: Start SMN-directed disease-modifying therapy as early as possible using the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec gene-replacement therapy, or the oral SMN2 splicing modifier risdiplam
Act on a newborn-screening or presymptomatic diagnosis to begin therapy before irreversible anterior-horn motor-neuron loss
Provide proactive respiratory care with non-invasive ventilation, airway-clearance and cough-assist techniques, and prompt treatment of chest infections
Optimise nutrition and swallowing safety, using gastrostomy feeding where bulbar weakness threatens aspiration
Manage musculoskeletal complications with physiotherapy, orthoses and monitoring and treatment of scoliosis and contractures
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, respiratory, orthopaedics, dietetics and rehabilitation, with anticipatory and palliative planning in the most severe infantile form
Monitor motor function with standardised scales to assess response to disease-modifying therapy
Offer genetic counselling with SMN2 copy-number-informed prognosis and carrier and family screening
